Great Depression. From nineteen twenty-nine to nineteen thirty-nine, the worst economic catastrophe of the twentieth century unfolded. Triggered by the stock market crash in October nineteen twenty-nine and deepened by bank failures, agricultural collapse, and deflationary spirals, it ravaged the developed world, destabilized democracies, fueled fascism, and fundamentally transformed how governments understood their role in economic management.

The nineteen-twenties had seen speculative euphoria in the stock market. Americans bought stocks on margin, borrowing to invest, inflating prices far above underlying corporate value. On Black Tuesday, October twenty-ninth, nineteen twenty-nine, the stock market crashed catastrophically. Stocks lost forty percent of their value within weeks, wiping out fortunes and destroying credit. This triggered a cascade of defaults and bankruptcies.

The crash exposed deeper weaknesses: unequal income distribution, overproduction of agricultural goods, international debt from World War One, and the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of nineteen thirty, which raised U.S. import duties and provoked retaliation, collapsing international trade.

Bank failures cascaded across America. As depositors panicked and withdrew savings, thousands of banks failed because they had loaned out more than they held in reserves. With no FDIC insurance, depositors lost everything. Agricultural collapse devastated farmers as commodity prices plummeted. The Dust Bowl of the nineteen-thirties compounded this misery with severe drought and soil erosion across the Great Plains, driving tenant farmers westward to California.

Industrial production fell by fifty percent. Unemployment in the United States reached twenty-five percent, higher in industrial cities. Millions lost homes to foreclosure. Bread lines and Hoovervilles, shanty towns, became symbols of American destitution.

The Depression destabilized democracies worldwide. Hitler rose to power partly by promising to restore German economic vitality. Militarism in Japan was fueled by economic desperation. In America, President Hoover's belief in limited government prevented aggressive federal intervention. Voters rejected him in nineteen thirty-two, electing Franklin D. Roosevelt, who promised active government intervention.

Roosevelt's New Deal from nineteen thirty-three to nineteen thirty-nine fundamentally expanded federal power. The Work Progress Administration employed millions in public works. The Civilian Conservation Corps restored forests and built infrastructure. Social Security in nineteen thirty-five created a safety net for the elderly and unemployed.

The Depression inspired a generation of artists and writers to document American suffering. Photographers Walker Evans and Dorothea Lange captured migrant workers and displaced families. John Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath became the Depression's literary epitaph. Folk musician Woody Guthrie gave voice to working-class America. John Maynard Keynes published The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money in nineteen thirty-six, arguing that government spending could stimulate demand and end recessions, a revolutionary idea that transformed economic policy.

The Depression began lifting in the mid-nineteen-thirties, partly from New Deal programs and more decisively from World War Two's rearmament and industrial mobilization in the early nineteen-forties. Its political legacy was profound: it discredited laissez-faire economics and established the expectation that government must intervene in recessions to prevent mass suffering. The Depression remained a benchmark of economic catastrophe, its specter haunting policymakers during the two thousand eight financial crisis.
